abstract: Organisms expand their metabolism by repurposing promiscuous enzymes to perform new reactions. To be repurposed, an enzyme often must balance its original and new functions-If it cannot, another promiscuous candidate may be recruited instead. Here, we investigate how metabolic evolution of a glucokinase-deficient bacterium is impacted by environmental changes wherein the canonical substrate of the preferred recruitment candidate, N-acetyl-D-mannosamine kinase (NanK), is gradually depleted while a new resource, glucose, is abundantly available. Despite the presence of three additional genomically encoded promiscuous glucokinases, we find that NanK is still recruited to restore glycolysis via two distinct mechanisms that leave native activity largely unaltered. In one mechanism, small-scale gene amplification precedes the appearance of two non-synonymous mutations in nanK that increase glucokinase activity but have little or no effect on N-acetyl-D-mannosamine kinase activity. In another mechanism, recruitment occurs via amplification of a ∼1000 base pair fragment that narrowly encompasses nanK and reaches copy numbers as high as 127. Despite maintenance of amplification for hundreds of generations, we observe no persistent mutations in any nanK duplicate at the level of resolution provided by 75X whole genome sequencing coverage. Our results demonstrate that variable selection for multiple functions does not prevent recruitment of the preferred glucokinase candidate despite the existence of other, seemingly equal candidates. Our findings also reveal that evolution by the Innovation-Amplification-Divergence model may only be facilitated at moderate levels of gene amplification, and hindered by massive amplification, as increased gene copy number diminishes returns of individual adaptive point mutations.
